operations.comment: ; Reading guide: mapper 2 lower 16KiB bank 0 contains encounter/audio code; the upper
;16KiB is fixed physical PRG banks 14/15. Six middle banks are non-code assets.
; CPU addresses in names/operands are execution aliases. Physical comments and
; incbin offsets preserve storage identities, including the 16-byte iNES header.
; All Unknown spans remain opaque. A named read alias inside one does not classify
; its bytes or establish the full extent of a table. Calls may cross opaque spans.
; Generic Work fields are shared scratch, not persistent game objects. Many actor
; arrays have two fighter entries; X2/3 are projectile/render slots. Music voices
; use a 20-byte stride; the aliases below name the first voice. Board/AI routines
; reuse movement timers as piece counters and several scratch fields as pointers.
; This listing describes the classified paths, not a complete game implementation.
; CPU RAM, hardware registers and established table read aliases.
; bank 0 table, physical $00ABF
; interior TXA entry documented at RenderActorFromIndex
; Additional mechanical fields. AI candidate arrays overlap the demonstration workspace.
; iNES header: mapper 2, 128KiB PRG, CHR RAM and vertical mirroring. Preserve all 16 original bytes.

; Build the arena encounter from the selected board square and the two piece IDs. Preserve the board origin, choose each actor type and starting strength, load arena graphics, and arrange the two fighters. X indexes the two sides. Several calls consume classified inline Data records and resume after them according to the helper stack contracts.
; Clear both strength accumulators before choosing the terrain palette and the two fighters. Type $0C borrows the opposing type; the strength adjustment also depends on the board square and side.
; Palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-out helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Use actor type to initialize capability, movement and strength fields. Terrain adds or subtracts a small strength adjustment before the per-side state arrays are cleared.

; Place fighters at opposite horizontal edges with the same vertical coordinate, then animate them toward the entrance positions. Establish three terrain phase thresholds relative to the fixed-bank terrain constant.

; Choose three groups of obstacle positions. Cycle the low quadrant selector, reject coordinates outside the interior or occupied cells, then set the high quadrant bits for three placements per group. X counts accepted candidates; rejected coordinates retry without consuming it.
; Count nonzero piece-strength entries in the two 18-piece groups. The difference biases the computer fighter parameters; these are counts of pieces, not occupied board coordinates.
; Clear movement timers, collision states and AI accumulators before the first fighter update. Returning from combat copies remaining fighter strength back to the board piece slots.

; For each real piece ID, commit the arena strength to the persistent piece table. A zero-strength piece also clears its matching remembered ID. Restore the saved board cursor and selected-piece coordinates before returning to board display.

; Select the surviving side from remaining strength, save the caller return bytes in that side's actor fields, hide the other fighter and clear its two 48-byte pattern spans through the NMI transfer buffer. This consumes the caller stack pair deliberately; it is not an ordinary balanced leaf call.

; Choose a result palette from encounter outcome and terrain phase, stop music, restore the board display and markers, then continue the next board turn. Inline palette arguments are skipped by their stack-reading helpers.
; Palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-out helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-out helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-out helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Target palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-in helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Preserve A while testing the central row and edge columns. The special square calls the fixed-bank modifier; the adjustment is returned through WorkAdjustment. X selects the encounter side.

; Three twenty-byte actor-type arrays configure computer attack reach, avoidance distance and extra avoidance thresholds. CPU $82C6/$82D4/$82ED load $0674,X/$0676,X/$067A,X respectively. The third value also supplies $0678,X after adding three; it is not derived from $0676,X.

; Disable rendering, then choose three groups of six random obstacle positions. Reject out-of-range random nibbles and duplicate cells; each accepted position writes a 2 by 2 tile block. Restore the display when placement finishes.

; Convert candidate cell coordinates to pixels and scan the stored coordinate pairs at $0100 for duplicates. Append a new pair, compute its nametable address, and emit four consecutive tiles in two rows. This use of page 1 coexists with the stack; the list is bounded by the caller.
; For each of three obstacle phase values, store 0, $40 or $80 according to zero and low-nibble phase two. These flags feed the direction-mask resolver; the exact visual phase names remain uncertain.
; Read the stored obstacle coordinate pairs, convert pixels back to cells, and update the attribute buffer. The loop processes $24 coordinate bytes.
; VRAM destination low/high and one-byte transfer count; bytes already reside in the transfer buffer. The helper skips all 3 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Derive an attribute-byte index and quadrant from the cell coordinates. Preserve X/Y; mask the old quadrant and insert the corresponding two-bit palette selection using the small table at $866C.
; Four complementary clear masks followed by four single-quadrant set masks. Indexed actor/obstacle code combines these with packed sprite attribute fields.
; Wait for display updates while repeatedly servicing the obstacle animation. The counter is stored on the stack around the service call; the observed PLA/TXA sequence is retained exactly.
; Hide sprite groups by setting every fourth OAM byte to $F0. Fall through to hide the smaller groups as well.
; Hide the two small OAM groups beginning at $0218 and $0258 by replacing their Y coordinates.
; Read a zero-terminated tile sequence. Queue one tile per frame, advance the PPU destination by one row, and stop at the zero terminator.
; Four zero-terminated sprite tile sequences alternate seven and eight bytes. The indexed emitter consumes them; the following byte at physical $006F8 starts code rather than a fifth sequence.

; Leave through the shared return when the action is finished; otherwise test computer-side and turn state before continuing the arena loop. The CPU alias belongs to the lower bank-zero execution view.
; Visit the two fighters and their two projectiles. Select the appropriate renderer/collision handler, mark combat finished when a fighter has no strength, then service hit and obstacle collisions.
; When both direction bits are set, collapse the temporary flags into an actor animation state and clear the temporary direction accumulator.
; Run projectile-versus-opponent checks and then obstacle collisions. Projectile damage resolution and phase handling use the shared actor arrays.

; Retain signed collision latches and derive three flags from terrain phase differences. Zero or difference two maps to zero; the other differences select $40/$80. The following obstacle tick consumes these flags.
; At the slow frame boundary, adjust obstacle phase bytes toward their next value. Low-nibble endpoints reverse the direction, while the high phase bits are retained.

; For each side, update an existing projectile first. A living fighter uses either computer control or its controller directions. Fire is accepted only when motion permits and the actor type supports it; cooldown and turn ownership are then updated.

; Read the controller belonging to X modulo 2. Direction masks $80/$40/$10/$20 select the four movement handlers. Keep the original input byte on the stack so multiple direction tests see the same sample.

; Reject attack when this update already moved the fighter. Button A is bit 0; only the applicable actor class enters the special attack helper. Movement animation advances once per eight motion ticks.
; Service attacks, decrement the per-side cooldown, and queue a sound when it expires. In the single-controller mode, hand control to the other side after processing this fighter.
; Tail-call the sound-effect selector with actor type plus twenty. X retains the fighter/effect channel selection.
; Reject movement during cooldown. Depending on frame parity, accumulate horizontal direction flags or enter the movement/projectile setup path.
; Set the facing animation, derive the projectile horizontal origin from the fighter, and copy its capability byte. Actor type $0F applies an origin correction.
; Reject movement during cooldown. Accumulate left-facing flags on alternating frames; otherwise move left subject to the arena edge and set the corresponding animation.
; Mark an attack request, choose the projectile origin and set the left-facing attack state. The shared direction formatter supplies diagonal flags and offsets.
; Start the projectile below the fighter. Type $0F applies a six-pixel correction; preserve this mechanical distinction without assigning a weapon name.

; When control/cooldown permits, step the fighter vertically toward the upper limit. On attack input, set the attack state, vertical projectile origin and directional motion. Shared continuation resolves diagonal sprite flags and offsets.

; Mirror the upward path at the lower limit. An attack sets the down-facing state, copies its horizontal increment and positions the projectile below the actor; diagonal motion uses the shared direction formatter.
; Combine horizontal and vertical signs into projectile and actor sprite flags. Select a two-entry signed origin adjustment from horizontal direction and add it to the projectile's vertical position.
; Return from the arena movement path; the following direction adjustments are data.

; Two Y-origin adjustments selected by ProjectileDeltaX sign: negative selects index 0, nonnegative index 1. CPU $8A9D starts Y at zero and increments only for a nonnegative delta. Both entries are zero, so the addition preserves ProjectileOriginY.
; When a control handler requested an attack, queue the type-specific sound, reset attack state and load the cooldown table. Capability bits choose the projectile activation format.
; Clear animation motion, mark the projectile active and copy the fighter origin. Type fourteen instead initializes its phase to $29 and enters the special rotating path.
; Set the active projectile byte and check a short actor-type table to choose whether its direction field is cleared. The type table determines the exceptional direction-reset cases.

; At phase five, resolve a hit; at phase ten reset the phase and advance a five-byte template offset. Read the sprite flags and relative offsets from the selected record. Earlier reads are overwritten, so their game meaning is not inferred.
; Advance a modulo-five phase and periodically resolve a hit. Select one of four tile flags from the upper phase bits, place the projectile at the fighter origin minus four horizontally, then return.
; Four direction-selected projectile tile flags: $C8,$D8,$E8,$D8. The rotating projectile path indexes these with two phase bits.
; Choose the OAM group from vertical ordering and hide sixteen sprites by writing $F0 to every Y byte. Continue through the common projectile clear path.

; Five five-byte projectile animation records. The consumer selects a record at a multiple of five and uses its sprite flag and relative X/Y bytes; earlier record reads are overwritten. Do not infer a separate effect from those discarded reads.
; At a matching collision latch and final lifetime nibble, resolve the projectile hit and optionally play the opponent effect. Decrement the lifetime; zero enters the shared clear path.
; Skip inactive projectiles. Capability bit $40 dispatches to the phase-based handler; other formats use the movement/collision helpers and their per-side collision state.

; Resolve signed hit state, special projectile behavior and movement increments. Clear projectiles outside the horizontal/vertical arena bounds; inside bounds, tick animation every fourth update. Shared entries preserve the earlier return and cooldown paths.
; Return from the active-projectile update; the following capability selectors are Data.
; Eight actor-type selectors used by adjacent projectile/capability tests. The values are type IDs rather than execution addresses.
; Hide the projectile, redraw its slot, clear activity/origins and motion counters, then normalize attack animations back to ordinary movement states.
; Map one attack animation to its corresponding resting state; the other arms preserve the encoded direction bit when choosing the default state.

; Check the attacker's collision-side mask, actor type and defender strength. Subtract attack damage, cancel the defender projectile when required, and on defeat stop its animation, clear uploaded patterns and move it offscreen. Store the resulting collision latch for the attacker; zero/sign carry distinct outcomes.
; For each slot X down to zero, scan at most four low direction bits. The first set bit selects an obstacle flag; fighter slots exclude the fourth direction. Store zero when no accepted bit is found.
; Shift actor coordinates by eight, wrapping the vertical edge back by sixteen. Clear step timers; the special actor/projectile case also relocates its sprite origin through the shared path.

; Move the low phase nibble in steps of two, preserving the high nibble. Reverse direction at zero/fourteen; later obstacle slots skip phases four and ten. This mirrors the fixed-bank terrain oscillator without proving a particular terrain name.

; Use the actor-indexed page byte as the high address, set the low byte to zero and clear all 256 bytes through an indirect pointer. The caller must initialize the page selector; no ROM upload origin is implied.
; Call the same projectile/opponent collision test for both sides, preserving the caller X. X identifies the projectile owner and Y the opposing fighter.

; Skip inactive projectiles and dispatch the two special actor types separately. Other types compare the projectile and opponent positions, with a six-pixel vertical adjustment in the classified comparison arm.
; Store the projectile collision result in the indexed actor state. CheckProjectileAgainstOpponent supplies Work0 on the opponent-test path; the other path supplies its collision value directly.

; Restore the saved owner/opponent indexes and compute the signed vertical separation from projectile to opponent. Compare the position differences against type-dependent hit bounds before storing the collision latch.
; Save both actor indexes, select an actor from A and call the sprite visibility/type helper. Use separate bounding boxes for visible and special sprite forms before storing the shared hit result.

; Choose an OAM group by vertical order. Build four columns and four rows at eight-pixel spacing, then fill sixteen sequential tile IDs and side attributes. Scratch fields hold base coordinates and the first tile.
; Check all four actor/projectile slots against the stored obstacle coordinate pairs.
; Quantize the actor position to a 16-pixel cell, with a different vertical bias for fighters and projectiles. Search the obstacle coordinate list and inspect the corresponding animated phase nibble.
; Continue scanning backward through coordinate pairs; clear the indexed collision state if no matching obstacle is found.
; Compare the two fighters' vertical positions and XOR that order with X to select one of two 64-byte OAM groups. Return its byte offset in Y; this is sprite ordering, not physical ROM banking.

; Initialize separation signs and AI flags, service a pending special-action counter, then use opponent distance, weapon reach, cooldown and obstacle state to select motion or attack. Positive/negative motion counters encode opposite directions.
; Strip the sign bit when deciding whether a directional counter is exhausted. If a movement remains active, execute it; otherwise derive a fresh cell position and opponent separation.
; Convert the current fighter position to arena cells. Subtract fighter coordinates from the opponent, recording absolute horizontal/vertical distance and a sign flag for each axis.

; Compare vertical and horizontal separation with the per-type reach threshold. Nearly aligned fighters choose a direct pursuit/attack arm; other cases examine opponent projectiles and choose an approach axis.
; Choose the opposing slot by XOR1. An active opposing projectile selects an evasion arm; otherwise use separation and edge alignment to approach.
; Compare both fighters reach and the secondary distance thresholds before calling the vertical/horizontal approach helpers. The pending-result flag can divert to obstacle handling.

; Convert opponent position to an arena cell, compare with the candidate row and probe intermediate cells along the vertical route. Set signed up/down step flags after shifting the obstruction result; equal positions fall back to relative direction.

; Compare opponent horizontal cell against the candidate column, probe each intervening permitted cell and select a signed horizontal step. Shared obstruction flags decide whether the route remains usable.
; Inspect the opposing projectile and current actor type while an attack cooldown is active. Choose a distance-based evasion path, subject to projectile activity and the opponent cooldown.
; Compare the opponent separation against the two per-type avoidance thresholds. A special actor class and its cooldown alter which movement helper runs.

; Compare vertical separation against the avoidance threshold, then try vertical and horizontal movement in opponent-relative order. Retry an alternate axis when the obstruction flag rejects the first trial.

; Select upward/downward trial from relative position and reach limits. Check arena edges and intervening obstacle cells before recording an eight-pixel vertical step and calling the shared motion path.
; Use the horizontal sign flag to choose an approach direction. Compare distance with the avoidance threshold and respect arena bounds before checking the adjacent cell.
; Check reach, opponent direction and the left screen edge. Reject blocked adjacent cells, then start a signed eight-tick horizontal step and update the cached cell coordinate.
; Check the right edge and cell parity before starting the corresponding positive horizontal step. The shared cell probe rejects an occupied adjacent cell before accepting the step.
; Draw a pseudorandom value for this AI decision arm. Use its low bits to choose an initial obstacle-response direction.
; Try obstacle-response movement on both axes in randomized order. A failed trial permits the opposite direction; the decision flag controls retries and whether the chosen movement is executed.
; Advance each signed direction counter toward its terminal magnitude and invoke the matching arena movement handler. The sign distinguishes opposing directions; zero means no pending step.
; Save A, subtract the arena origin, divide by 16 and round by the original low nibble. Return the cell in CandidateRow; WorkValue retains the original pixel coordinate.

; Inspect the proposed cell through a temporary pointer. Occupancy and signed terrain entries decide whether to return normally or discard an extra return address, abandoning the caller move attempt. The caller supplies the candidate cell, side and movement fields reused by this probe.

; Message pointer words and $FE/$FF-terminated tile/text strings precede the actor tables. Existing named aliases identify per-type capability, strength, movement and cooldown arrays and the per-ID type map. Generic portions retain the envelope boundary; the original container's complete subdivisions are unresolved.

; Build several sprite groups from small layout templates and indexed frame tables. Wait between frames, allow Start to exit, and wrap the frame index after eleven entries. Music activity controls one display-register sequence.

; Sprite templates contain tile, attribute and relative coordinate bytes. The nearby template emitters choose different starting offsets; these are shared layouts rather than independent code entries.
; Select nine sprite records and share the same template renderer as the twelve-record entry.
; Emit OAM records from triples of Y offset, tile offset and X offset. Add the supplied group origin and tile base; a tile base at or above $F0 hides the entire group instead.
; Write $F0 to each selected OAM Y byte, skipping the remaining three fields. The shared count bounds the group.

; Small repeated fields next to the sprite emitters were inspected with those consumers. Their exact schema and complete consumer relationship remain unresolved; retain this non-code envelope without invented record names.

; Hide sprites, set the credits palette and clear the nametable in 64-byte buffered spans. Reveal fixed 32-byte text rows with inline descriptors. Wait up to 128 iterations or Start, then stop music and fade out. Text helpers can unwind the credits caller on Start.
; Palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-out helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Target palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-in helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the left-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the right-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the left-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the right-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the left-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the left-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the right-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the left-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the right-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the right-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the right-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Text source pointer and VRAM destination, both little endian, for the left-side row reveal. The helper skips all 4 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-out helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Sixteen NES palette bytes in four four-color groups. Credits setup selects this palette through the inline fade helper.
; A 512-byte, space-padded credits text matrix. Credits reveal helpers read 32-byte rows from pointers in their inline descriptors. Preserve the local text and copyright notices in the binary asset.

; Consume four inline bytes: source pointer and VRAM destination. Clear a 32-byte row, then progressively move the source text in from the right. Service input/frames between stages; Start removes this helper's return pair and exits the credits sequence.

; Consume the same four-byte source/destination descriptor and slide the source suffix into a cleared 32-byte row. Its shared Start exit unwinds to the credits finish path. Each stage queues one buffered row.

; Advance a palette phase and copy sixteen bytes into the transfer buffer, temporarily preserving transfer destination/count. Queue the palette transfer and restore those fields before the adjacent decimal conversion helper.
; Repeatedly subtract ten from A; return quotient in Work0 and remainder in Work1. X is the tens counter. The preceding palette helper falls through into this conversion using its restored count.

; Disable rendering, select VRAM $2108 and emit nine alternating sixteen-tile ramps and solid rows. Restore PPU control/mask shadows afterward. Static entry is supported; normal game usage remains uncertain.
; Write sixteen tile values starting at X to PPUDATA, incrementing X for each. The caller owns the PPU address and rendering state.
; Write sixteen $F2 tiles to PPUDATA. The caller owns the PPU address and rendering state.

; Disable rendering and fill thirty nametable rows with alternating pairs from a four-byte tile set, then restore display control. Direct PPU writes require the controlled rendering interval established here.
; Four literal tiles $20..$23 used by the direct checkerboard writer. Their arrangement is selected by four fixed reads rather than a pointer table.

; Queue ten transfers starting at VRAM $218A with a $20-byte destination stride, waiting two frames per row. The buffer-clear helper initializes eleven bytes although the transfer count is sixteen; callers retain responsibility for the remaining buffer bytes.
; Clear transfer-buffer offsets ten through zero. This helper does not clear the entire sixteen-byte queued row.
; Disable rendering and write tile $27 exactly 960 times to VRAM $2000. The $03BF counter is inclusive through zero. Follow with a six-byte direct-upload descriptor; this is not a 1024-byte clear.
; Source pointer, VRAM destination and sixteen-bit count for the direct PPU copy. The helper skips all 6 bytes when restoring the return address.

; Choose a forward or backward twelve-byte stride through the palette matrix. For ten stages, insert universal color $0F before each three-color group and queue sixteen palette bytes. The alternate entry selects the other endpoint and stride.

; Ten twelve-byte palette stages. The transition inserts $0F before each triple to form four-color groups, traversing the matrix with signed strides of twelve. The isolated return byte after this envelope remains Unknown.

; Alternate timed PPU control and scroll writes between two nametables. Increase one horizontal offset by three and decrease the other until the latter wraps toward two; short loops provide instruction-count delays. Exact scanline timing is not asserted.
; Draw the transition rows, then continue the title/game control loop.
; Delay with an outer count in A and sixteen-decrement inner loops. Clobbers the shared outer counter and X; duration depends on the CPU execution timing.

; Select a three-byte descriptor by option index: little-endian source pointer and number of zero-terminated text lines. Copy each line into the transfer buffer, queue it and advance VRAM by $40. Clear the surrounding option panel first.

; Three-byte menu descriptors select a text pointer and line count. Zero-terminated option strings follow, then a sixteen-byte cursor bitmap. The option drawing consumer establishes the descriptor stride and string termination.
; Draw a sixteen-tile top border, eight interior rows and a bottom border starting at VRAM $2188. The interior loop preserves side bytes in the transfer buffer while replacing its middle with spaces.

; Load the options display, copy its initial state, and ask for player/control and side choices. Store the selected computer-controller mask and initial side polarity. A timeout diverts to demonstration setup.
; Inline memory-copy record: source $A5A5, destination $0302, length $10. CopyMemoryInline advances the stacked return by 5; this is data even when embedded between instructions.

; Move the option cursor, wait for input release and sample controller 0. Up/down clamp the selection between zero and the supplied maximum. A slow timeout discards a return address and switches to demonstration mode.
; Discard the caller return address, reset the timeout and mark both demonstration flags. This nonlocal exit belongs to the options timeout path.
; Poll the controller until any button is nonzero, returning the sampled buttons. The adjacent helper separately waits until all buttons are released.
; Wait a display frame and poll controller 0 until all accepted input bits are released.
; Wait for a nonzero input, preserve that sample across the release wait and return it to the option handler.
; Build the first sprite record. The selected menu row multiplied by 16 plus $70 supplies its Y coordinate; tile, attributes and X stay fixed.

; Convert the 16-bit turn counter by repeated subtraction of decimal place values. Emit five ASCII digits, replace leading zeroes with spaces except the last, then queue the count and TURNS label through inline descriptors.
; Source pointer, RAM destination and one-byte count for the memory copy. The helper skips all 5 bytes when restoring the return address.
; VRAM destination low/high and one-byte transfer count; bytes already reside in the transfer buffer. The helper skips all 3 bytes when restoring the return address.
; High-byte and low-byte decimal place-value arrays feed the turn-counter conversion; literal TURNS text follows. Pointer aliases into this envelope do not imply executable entries.
; Draw a pair of vertical tile bars using buffered incrementing transfers and a shared palette descriptor. The alternate entry accepts a low destination offset in A.
; Source pointer, VRAM destination and one-byte count for the buffered copy. The helper skips all 5 bytes when restoring the return address.

; Clear forty bytes of secondary channel state and shared counters, set voice register offsets to 0/4/8, initialize envelope sentinels and enable the four APU channels. The music-active flag remains zero until a sequence starts.
; Clear music activity, wait for a frame, silence the two pulse channels and disable triangle output.
; Use Y to select a ten-byte descriptor containing stream/table pointers. Reset three 20-byte channel states and the percussion cursor, enable the sequence, then decode its first percussion pattern.
; Start sequence zero, then repeatedly tick its channels and wait for a frame. This is a nonreturning static service entry; it does not establish a normal gameplay call route.
; When music is active, tick three channel records at offsets 0/$14/$28, then percussion, modulation, envelopes and triangle gating. Runs from the NMI while bank 0 is selected.
; Visit the three 20-byte channel records. Only active waveform/channel records need volume or triangle gate work.
; Compare current and target level; mute triangle on one side of the threshold and enable it on the other. Clamp the stored level when the target is reached.

; For an active channel, move its current level toward the target using the configured rise/fall increments. Combine the scaled level with duty/control bits and write the indexed APU channel register.

; Decrement note duration and gate counters. On expiry, fetch the next byte from the channel stream: ordinary bytes encode note/octave, duration commands update timers, and high commands dispatch through a handler table.
; Advance the channel stream pointer by A, read the next token and decode note/octave. Reload note and gate duration and schedule the period update before committing the stream pointer.
; Store stream pointer plus one back into the channel record. This is the common return after accepting a token.
; Values below the high command group index parallel duration tables. Store both live and reload duration counters, then advance the stream.
; Two indexed byte arrays supply low/high note-duration values to the channel stream decoder. Repeated values encode duration choices; their exact musical naming is unresolved.
; For commands $F7..$FF, subtract $F7, double the result and jump through the nine-word handler table. Values $F0..$F6 do not gain a valid-command contract from this dispatch.
; Nine little-endian command-handler pointers for bytes $F7..$FF. The dispatcher subtracts $F7 and doubles the result. This table does not make $F0..$F6 valid commands.
; Read one following byte and copy it to both live duration counters, then resume decoding two bytes after the token.
; Read two bytes after the command into the duration pair, then advance the stream by three bytes including the command.
; Save the address immediately after this command in the voice's loop pointer, then advance by one byte.
; Initialize or decrement the per-voice repeat count. While repetitions remain, restore the saved loop pointer; otherwise skip the command and count byte. Zero repeat operand exits without looping.
; Read the following byte, scale it by four and store the target envelope level before advancing two stream bytes.
; Use the following byte to select a four-byte instrument record: rising step, falling step, control/duty flags and modulation selector.
; Ten four-byte sound-envelope presets. The instrument command multiplies its index by four and loads four channel fields; the exact instrument names are unknown.
; Copy the following stream byte into the voice modulation parameter and advance by two bytes.
; Read a little-endian destination from the next two stream bytes and replace the active pointer. Continue parsing without an extra pointer increment.
; Clear the active music flag, silence both pulse channels and triangle output, discard the parser's return pair and return to its caller. This command deliberately unwinds one nested call.
; Advance a six-entry modulation cycle and store its current period offset. The low-nibble mask keeps the cursor bounded after wrap.
; Six modulation-step constants: $10,$0C,$08,$00,$08,$0C. The neighboring audio consumer uses this symmetric parameter sequence.
; Visit all three channel records; enabled modulation derives a note period from the note-table pair and adds the cyclic offset before octave scaling.
; Preserve channel state, derive a period from note and octave, and write duty/control, timer low/high and sweep to the indexed APU channel. The high timer includes the fixed length bits.

; Twelve little-endian pulse timer periods, descending from $06AE to $0389. The note writer adjusts octave and sends the resulting period to pulse timer registers; a specific tuning system is not asserted.

; Decrement the percussion duration. At expiry read a packed pattern byte: low nibble is duration and enabled high bits choose a four-register noise-channel preset. Advance the 16-step pattern cursor.

; Read the percussion sequence. A negative token redirects the sequence pointer; a positive token chooses a 16-byte pattern relative to the pattern-table base. Reset the pattern cursor after resolving the record.

; Channel configuration tuples, pointer/sequence descriptors and compact music streams. The known parser consumes note/duration fields and commands $F7..$FF through shared stream pointers. Internal boundaries and a complete song index remain unresolved, so unsegmented portions stay generic Data.
; Clear the two effect activity states, initialize pulse/noise controls and pulse high timers, and allow all three music voices plus percussion.
; Preserve the effect ID while stopping the prior effect. X parity selects one of two five-byte effect states; load the new stream descriptor and mute the music channels claimed by its mask.
; Use A as a two-byte pointer-table index. The descriptor first byte selects APU channels; initialize activity/countdown and advance to the first timed effect record.
; Rotate the effect channel mask to disable the corresponding music pulse/percussion enables. Other bits retain their original behavior; no unsupported channel interpretation is added.

; Effect pointer arrays and linked register/length descriptors with compact sound streams. The effect starter indexes this envelope and the playback consumer follows redirects and terminators. Exact sequence names and complete record subdivisions remain unresolved.
; Read the next two stream bytes as a new stream address and continue effect decoding. This is the $FF command path.
; Copy each saved five-byte effect state into the shared working fields, run one effect tick, and copy it back. The two streams share decoder code but retain independent pointers and countdowns.

; Skip inactive streams; decrement duration and fetch the next record when it expires. Zero ends the stream and $FF redirects it. Channel-mask bits determine which APU register payloads follow the duration byte.
; When the noise mask is set, copy three stream bytes to noise control, period and length registers, then advance the stream pointer by three.
; Restore music enable flags for channels claimed by the effect, silence the noise channel as needed, and clear effect activity. Preserve X around the restoration.

; Initialize the display and pulse registers, animate pulse volume and scripted sprites, play two bounded scripts, then silence channels and hide sprite memory. Uses private $0500-range state; this static sequence does not prove a natural entry route.
; Save Y in the demonstration delay field, wait Y frames and return. A zero input would wrap the decrement loop; callers here supply nonzero counts.

; Queue the turn/timing indicator, render its low-nibble decimal value and choose an automatic computer wait or human press/release polling from current-side control. Inline spans select the destination and digit framing.

; Established non-code uniform $FF bytes. Neighbor boundaries were inspected; original padding/reservation purpose is unknown. Keep as binary data rather than inventing a table.

; Spell-menu text, repeated tile-map fields, attribute values and palettes. Metatile/attribute upload consumers and inline pointers establish the non-code envelope. The following isolated return byte remains Unknown.
; Load the selected board-row pointer, use the column as index and write the selected piece ID. This helper performs the physical board update; callers establish its legality.

; Request a source selection, optionally initialize a computer-chosen target, then request the destination in mode $81. Clear the original board cell after accepted selection; selection/animation helpers own validity checks and completion flags.

; Store the supplied status, display its message and wait through the shared frame-service helper. Multiple action handlers use this common success/error tail.
; Invert the terrain direction field and display status nine through the common result tail. This changes phase direction, not the phase value itself.

; Select two occupied squares, save both piece IDs and clear both cells. After a redraw/delay, write the pieces into opposite cells through the row-pointer writer. Shared selection modes constrain ownership and legality.

; Require an eligible neighboring square, collect up to eight distinct dead piece types for the side and draw their list. Let the player select a type and destination, restore the chosen piece to maximum strength and rebuild its graphics/sprites. Empty lists and invalid placement use the shared failure flow.
; Convert the supplied type to a four-byte metatile record at $D93E+type*4. Arrange its top and bottom pairs in the transfer buffer at row offsets zero and $20. Preserve Y across the helper.

; Copy the initial attribute buffer, then set side-dependent masks in eight-byte strides according to the revival-list count. Full pairs and an odd last item use distinct masks before a descriptor-selected transfer.
; Source pointer, RAM destination and one-byte count for the memory copy. The helper skips all 5 bytes when restoring the return address.
; VRAM destination low/high and one-byte transfer count; bytes already reside in the transfer buffer. The helper skips all 3 bytes when restoring the return address.

; Reject the side's phase endpoint, otherwise select an opposing piece and store it in the side-specific restricted-piece slot. Successful selection uses the common status tail; phase rejection enters the action refund/retry path.

; Check occupied squares while excluding key-square indices, then choose one of four elemental IDs without repeating the last choice. Install its palette/strength, upload the special graphics tail and request a destination in mode $83. Type eighteen receives the extra animation flag. Further arena behavior remains in shared selection/action code.
; VRAM destination low/high and one-byte transfer count; bytes already reside in the transfer buffer. The helper skips all 3 bytes when restoring the return address.

; Initialize choice zero, require a released confirm button, then poll confirm and directional bits. Return choice in Y on confirm; movement handlers wrap eight menu rows while skipping used spell slots, with row seven reserved for cancellation.
; Rate-limit reverse selection with the low four repeat bits. Wrap below zero to seven, skip records marked $FE and redraw the choice; cancellation is always selectable.
; Rate-limit forward selection, wrap at eight and skip used spell records. Choice seven bypasses the spell-record read and enters the same redraw path.
; Clear the status span, then draw the selected action's message at a fixed text offset. Choice, text pointers and shared transfer scratch are reused by the calling menu loop.
; Generate the 3 by 3 coordinate neighborhood around the saved selected-piece origin. Store parallel column/row arrays, including out-of-board candidates for callers to reject.
; Clear messages, stop sound and mark the chosen side's action record $FD before finishing the turn through the common status path. This path is reached through an explicit cancellation unwind.
; Wait, restore the action record to $FD, display retry text and restore cursor/origin coordinates. Rebuild the actor position and return to the human selection flow after a short wait.

; Set the selection mode and service cursor/game input until action-finished is negative. Human cancel input unwinds to cancellation except in elemental mode. Invalid human selections either redisplay the saved message for selected action indices or unwind into refund/retry. Computer turns return directly after completion.
; Subtract one from the second actor's vertical pixel field. The shared board selection/effect callers use it before redrawing that actor.
; Resolve row Y through the board pointer arrays, use column A as index and store X into that cell. X can hold a piece ID or the $80 empty marker.
; Seven special-action record offsets followed by seven handler words. The computer action loop starts at six and decrements through zero, fixing the finite dispatch domain.

; Select the computer side, scan surviving pieces and skip its restricted piece. Load friendly/opponent ability tables, map IDs to coordinates and dispatch candidate special actions. The general search then scores eligible pieces and destination squares, retaining a best candidate with bounded random tie selection.
; Clear the scoring/selection work fields and count occupied board cells by side. Those counts feed endgame weighting before the positional, terrain and strength evaluation.

; Compare the two surviving-piece counts, store a side-relative count difference and adjust the timing state when both sides have fewer than three pieces. Counts below five also control the later endgame weighting flag.
; Scan the five key-square board indices, counting each side's occupants. Set the special weighting flag when either side owns four; empty squares do not increment either counter.

; Walk all 81 board cells, retaining allied pieces outside the restricted ID. Store piece IDs, board indices and baseline scores in parallel arrays. Scores combine central-square values, terrain and remaining spell availability.

; For each retained piece, recover row/column by division by nine, compute its current and missing strength, then enumerate destinations using its movement format. Save its best score and maintain the overall maximum.

; Compact candidates tied at the maximum score, randomly choose among the surviving entries using rejection bounds and restore the selected type, destination and origin coordinates. Parallel arrays carry IDs, board indices, scores and destination row/column.
; Convert selected destination cells to pixels, store the cursor target and read the piece movement-mode table before calling the movement evaluator.
; Return from the computer move selection path.

; Clamp the row range to 0..8 and shrink the horizontal reach by distance from the origin row. For each row, clamp its column range and run the shared square evaluator. The positive movement class produces a diamond-shaped search domain.
; Use the low movement nibble as range, clamp both coordinate intervals to 0..8 and evaluate every square in the rectangle. The sign-tagged movement class reaches this entry from the piece evaluator.

; Evaluate each candidate column on the current row. Reject invalid paths, subtract the origin baseline and keep higher scores; equal scores use a bounded random tie decision. Save the best destination in the piece's parallel row/column arrays.

; Compute row*9+column, evaluate terrain and spell adjustments and reject allied occupants. Enemy occupants add strength/damage terms; empty squares use positional weights. Shift the validity flag only on accepted square paths. Scores are byte arithmetic with the original carry dependencies preserved.
; When the power-square weighting flag is set, compare the board index against five key-square indices and add six on a match. Otherwise leave the current score unchanged.
; Map the cell's static color descriptor or current oscillating phase to a half-phase score. Invert around seven for the opposite computer side. X retains the board index.
; Count seven side-record entries equal to $FE starting at Y. Preserve X; return the count in the shared adjustment field. Cancellation is outside this seven-entry count.

; Square-position score weights and eighteen supported displacement values. The computer evaluator combines the positional table with terrain/strength terms, then matches route cases against the displacement array.

; Convert destination to a linear board index and match its absolute displacement against eighteen cases. Load route length, alternatives and final handler selector, choose sign-dependent delta variants and probe occupancy. Unsupported displacements use a direct one-square route fallback; finite selectors dispatch three route-adjustment handlers.

; Build route entries from origin plus signed deltas, checking board occupancy. Empty paths shift the validity flag after all cells; occupied paths advance the delta cursor without that success shift. X counts remaining route slots and the caller may retry an alternative.

; Signed board-step variants, four eighteen-entry route parameter arrays and three final handler words. Route selectors are $00,$02,$04 or negative; negative selectors skip the final dispatch. The three positive selectors are byte offsets into the pointer array.
; Build a one-entry route and move accepted cells among the three route slots. Retry selected delta variants when blocked, preserving the validity flag's success/failure convention.
; Probe several one-entry alternatives and reorder accepted results into route slots two and one. Shift the validity flag between stages; failed alternatives retry through the common probe.
; For short movement ranges skip a counted series of deltas, then initialize a one-entry route and probe it. Larger ranges enter the final probe directly.
; Use X as a two-byte action-handler index and jump through the stored pointer. No handler address is treated as new code classification merely because it appears here.

; Compare terrain phase, side polarity, remaining special-action entries and side state before considering the action. Thresholds differ by side; some strategic thresholds and original action names remain uncertain.
; Return from this eligibility path; adjacent unresolved arms are preserved.
; Jump to the common special-action commit helper, which consumes the chosen action entry and records its board coordinates.

; Search a side-dependent five-row/four-column rectangle for enemy pieces, excluding a key type. Save their IDs and maximum strengths, then choose a highest-strength target with a random minimum-index filter. Find its coordinates and shift the action decision flag on success.

; On one random case out of four, try two side-specific piece IDs through the key-square/terrain target checker. A successful checker can unwind this helper rather than continue to the second candidate.

; Require a surviving candidate, find its coordinates and reject a power-square case. Test its board-color descriptor against the computer side; an accepted target shifts the decision flag and removes the immediate caller return pair.
; Find the side-specific key piece, map its ID to a board cell, and test whether it is on one of the five special squares. Return the signed test result through DecisionFlag.

; Compare terrain direction and phase endpoints with side, imprisonment slots and action availability. Qualifying states jump to the shared special-action commit; other states return without committing. Several cases are mechanical heuristics whose strategic intent is uncertain.

; Try the key-piece and enemy-target helpers, then compare the selected target with the opponent restricted-piece slot and phase/color thresholds. Qualifying states commit the action; others return. Preserve the shared decision flag across helper calls.

; Try the key-piece route, then inspect restricted-piece/color thresholds and a side-dependent sequence of board positions. A friendly piece found by the delta scan becomes the stored action target; failed tests return without commit.
; Five signed board-index increments used by the side-dependent target scan. They are deltas, not CPU pointers.

; Occasionally select a random row and the side edge, then compare its occupied piece with the mirrored square and terrain. A movement-class exception evaluates a two-column search over all rows and retains a sufficiently high score. Commit stores the target coordinates and selected piece; unsuccessful candidates return.

; Build a nine-square neighborhood around the saved origin, reject out-of-board, occupied or power-square entries and test terrain for the active side. On a qualifying empty square, try side-specific dead piece IDs and commit the first eligible revival target.
; Require zero strength for candidate Y, save its ID and remove the caller pair before jumping to the common action commit. Living pieces return normally.
; Try a fixed side-specific set of two or three piece IDs through the low-strength healing predicate. Successful predicates unwind directly to the action commit.
; Require surviving strength below six, locate the piece and reject a power-square case. Qualifying targets discard the immediate caller return pair and commit; others return normally.

; Search the 81-cell board for the supplied piece ID. Divide the matching linear index by 9 to return column in A and row in Y, storing the index in WorkValue. Callers must supply a present ID; the miss case is not a validated contract.

; Mark the chosen special-action table entry $FE, shift the decision flag and record its effect/target coordinates. The seven-entry effect table routes the accepted choice to its shared animation/action continuation.

; Raise and redraw the actor, display side/action messages and delay before dispatching one of seven effect handlers with the established action index. Handler entries may be shared interior continuations rather than independent routines.
; Seven little-endian computer effect-handler pointers indexed by the established action index zero through six. Several targets intentionally share interior continuations or returns.
; Place the actor at the saved target and continue through the imprisonment selection/result path.
; Raise the actor one pixel and continue through the terrain-direction reversal path.
; Set the actor at the saved target and continue the elemental creation path.
; Position and raise the actor, then enter the common healing-selection path.
; Position and raise the actor, then enter the common teleport-selection path. The return entry at the end is shared by unused/no-op effect cases.
; Position the target, choose side-dependent pixel coordinates and load the saved dead piece ID/type before reusing the revival rendering/strength completion path.
; Convert the saved target to pixels, store horizontal destination and vertical destination minus one. Shared conversion updates the computer cursor target too.
; Convert the saved target to pixels and store the unadjusted two-coordinate destination.
; Load saved column/row into computer target fields and invoke board-cell-to-pixels for actor slot four. Return the horizontal pixel coordinate in A and vertical coordinate in Y.
; Reset turn counters and computer ownership, set default side/options and enable demonstration/initial-placement flags before entering shared game setup.

; Clear the turn counter, hide sprites and select bank two. Upload descriptor-selected blocks and draw the direct metatile screen, restore bank zero, fade the palette and reenable display/NMI control before continuing game initialization.
; Source pointer, VRAM destination and sixteen-bit count for the direct PPU copy. The helper skips all 6 bytes when restoring the return address.
; Source pointer, VRAM destination and sixteen-bit count for the direct PPU copy. The helper skips all 6 bytes when restoring the return address.

; Target palette pointer (little endian) for the fade-in helper. The helper skips all 2 bytes when restoring the return address.

; Queue the initial display/palette, run options, clear game RAM and construct piece strength and pointer tables. The two sides start from opposite board edges; the setup chooses between animated placement and the ordinary board loop.

; Fill all 81 board cells with $80, copy the chosen side polarity and terrain state, then choose animated placement or direct initial placement.
; Sixteen four-byte placement records. The placement loop advances by four and reads type/ID, board row, column and a related selector; no unverified original record names are imposed.
; Use four-byte placement records containing piece ID, count and board coordinates. Place each group, animate the associated sprites and alternate sides before entering the game board setup.
; Convert the placement cell to target pixels and write repeated piece IDs to successive board coordinates. Set a side-dependent sprite spacing and enter the shared placement animator.

; Place a group of actor sprites along the side edge, upload their graphics and display the piece message. Either controller can accelerate the placement; otherwise animate until the group reaches its target.
; Once finished, return through the common placement exit. Otherwise update the group animation counter and move each sprite toward the target, recording when all arrive.
; Choose a signed one-pixel step from side polarity, advance each sprite X toward the target, and set the action-complete flag when the entire group matches.
; Build per-sprite vertical positions, add the placement spacing and emit each group sprite template. A count in WorkValue bounds the number of pieces drawn.
; Select a side/frame-dependent template offset and pass actor pixels and a three-row count to the shared sprite renderer. Preserve the caller Y and template index around the call.
; Preserve X, fetch the current actor type and start its sound on effect slot 0.

; Redraw the board, clear remembered restrictions and lay out two occupied columns on each side of every row with five empty middle cells. Select the opposite starting side and enter the board-turn loop.
; Return from shared placement paths.

; Read two little-endian pointers from four bytes after JSR and advance the stacked return address. Expand 240 metatile indices through four-byte tile records into two-row transfer buffers. Upload 64 bytes per frame until the screen is complete.

; Select destination high byte $24 and enter the shared four-byte inline direct-screen renderer. The adjacent ordinary entry selects $20; their shared $3A store is intentional alternate-entry control flow.

; Read the same four-byte pointer pair, then disable rendering. Expand a 16 by 15 metatile map directly to the PPU, writing each top row before its bottom row. This helper changes the stacked return address by 4; inline bytes are never opcodes.

; Clear selected control bits and disable rendering before the shared six-byte inline attribute builder. The alternate entry starts after this setup and requires the caller to establish safe PPU state.

; Consume six inline bytes: lookup pointer, cell-map pointer and little-endian PPU destination. Gather four two-bit palette selectors from a 16-cell row stride into each attribute byte, building an 8x8 table in RAM. Upload 64 bytes directly, then restore rendering, NMI and zero scroll. The first selector is used unmasked exactly as encoded; callers must supply the expected lookup values.
; Remove a destination pair already prepared on the stack, then enter the four-byte inline loader. This entry requires that extra pair; an ordinary JSR alone does not supply its contract.

; Read four bytes after the remaining stacked return address into Work0..Work3, advance that return address by four with carry and jump through the prepared destination pointer. The inline bytes are parameters rather than fallthrough instructions.

; Read destination low/high and byte count from three bytes after JSR. Request a normal NMI upload, advance the return address by 3 and tail-call the frame wait. Current inline records are classified Data; their stack contracts determine continuation addresses.
; Compare the fighters Y coordinates to choose sprite ordering, combine it with side parity and fall through to actor rendering.

; Derive an OAM slot from X and select frame/tile/attribute data. Physical $1F684 is also an observed TXA entry inside the operand of BIT at $1F683; preserve that overlapping path without splitting the frozen classification.

; Combine animation base and frame, side parity and orientation into tile and attribute work fields. Fighters use a six-sprite template; projectile slots normally use a single OAM record, with a special selection-mode exception.
; Write one OAM record from the projectile coordinates, frame and side attributes. A nearby special-mode path selects a different projectile template.
; Use a two-frame animation to select a six-tile template, then share the fighter template renderer.

; Draw three rows of two sprites each, adding 8 pixels per row. A visibility helper can skip/hide a row, and the horizontal-flip flag selects the alternate layout. Keep the original OAM/tile progression; the alternate arms preserve the encoded tile order and coordinate increments.

; Build the alternate two-sprite row with vertically separated tiles and shared horizontal coordinate. Advance the horizontal origin by eight for each following pair; the sign-selected variant reverses tile progression.
; Compare the actor type against a three-entry list. For matching types, animation ranges determine the signed visibility result; other types return zero. No specific transformation name is assumed.
; Seven small capability constants. The sprite visibility code and special-opponent graphics routine read the first three entries; the exact role/domain of the remaining four is unresolved.
; Clear the NMI handshake and spin until NMI sets it. Requires NMI enabled and progressing; this is synchronization, not a free-running delay.
; Fill the OAM shadow with $F0 before changing scenes. Unlike a Y-only hide this replaces every byte.

; Store the desired lower 16KiB bank and preserve X. Write A to the matching selector byte in fixed ROM, avoiding a mapper 2 bus-conflict mismatch; restore X. The NMI restores this remembered bank after running bank 0 audio.
; Switch lower PRG bank without replacing SelectedPrgBank. NMI uses this entry while temporarily running the bank 0 audio routines; the ordinary entry first updates the remembered value.

; Read five inline bytes: source pointer, PPU destination and count. Copy count bytes backward into the transfer buffer, skip the five bytes on return, queue a normal transfer and wait for NMI. Count zero is not a safe empty-transfer contract.

; Read six inline bytes: source pointer, PPU destination and 16-bit count. Skip those bytes on return, disable rendering and transfer directly. The alternate entry at $F8C7 uses already prepared parameters. Reset scroll and control after the bounded copy.

; Clear the PPU increment/control bits used by the direct upload, set the VRAM destination, and copy through a 16-bit decrementing byte count. The caller must ensure rendering is disabled or tolerate the display transition.
; Restore the standard NMI/control value and zero both scroll writes and scroll shadows. Rendering enable is handled by callers.

; A chooses controller 0 or 1. Preserve X/Y and flags, strobe the selected port and collect eight bits into ControllerButtons. A nonzero mode flag redirects second-controller requests to the first-port path; the ordinary second-port path masks Select/Start. Returned bit 0 is A, bit 1 B, bit 4 Up, bit 5 Down, bit 6 Left, bit 7 Right.

; Copy seventeen literal seed bytes into RAM, adding the low frame clock with the existing carry chain. Preserve the original arithmetic; this establishes initialization mechanics without claiming a particular random-generator family.
; Seventeen initialization bytes copied into RAM with a frame-clock addition and retained carry chain. These seed the random state; no generator-family claim follows from the literal bytes.
; Shift a 17-byte state history, XOR four taps, store the new byte and return it in A. Preserve X; this is deterministic stateful pseudorandom generation.

; Read source pointer, destination pointer and one-byte length from five inline bytes, then skip them on return. Copy backward including offset 0. Length 0 follows the encoded wraparound behavior and is not interpreted as an empty copy.

; Copy the palette work buffer, apply each actor type's colors at offsets zero/four, then queue the resulting sixteen-byte palette span. Inline copy descriptors keep source, destination and bounds separate from execution flow.
; Source pointer, RAM destination and one-byte count for the memory copy. The helper skips all 5 bytes when restoring the return address.

; Copy a four-byte actor palette into the selected slot, then choose an additional palette record from actor type and slot. Preserve A/X so both sides share the helper.
; NES palette groups selected by actor palette consumers and fixed fade descriptors. Most groups begin with universal color $0F; exact game-scene names remain uncertain.

The IRQ vector also points here; that does not prove general IRQ compatibility.

; Copy the first transfer-buffer row, then reset the PPU address to destination plus$20 and copy the second row. The same count applies to both rows.

; Restore control and scroll, increment the two-byte frame clock, signal the frame waiter and service bank 0 music/effects. Bank restoration uses the saved lower-bank selection.
